chunks: And Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar wrote to Abu Muhammad (peace be upon him): Regarding

a man who bought a piece of land from another man with its four boundaries, and in it there was crops, palm trees, and other trees, but he did not mention the palm trees, the crops, or the trees in his deed, and he mentioned in it that he had bought it with all its rights, both those inside it and those outside it. Does this include the crops, palm trees, and trees within the rights of the land or not?
So he (peace be upon him) wrote: 'When one purchases the land with its boundaries and what is enclosed by its gate, then he has all that is in it, if God wills.'
And he also wrote to him:

A man bought an estate or a servant with money that he took from road robbery or from theft. Is it permissible for him to consume what comes to him from this estate, or is it permissible for him to have intercourse with this female slave whom he bought from theft or road robbery?
So he (peace be upon him) wrote: 'There is no good in anything whose origin is forbidden, and its use is not permissible.'
ai.seo_question: Are crops and trees included in the sale of land if not explicitly mentioned in the deed?
ai.summary: In this excerpt from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Shaykh al-Tusi records two juristic queries to Imam al-Hasan (AS) concerning the scope of property rights in land sales and the validity of using illicit wealth. The first ruling establishes that unspecified crops and trees are included if the land is sold with its encompassing boundaries and rights, reflecting the principle of *istishab* (presumption of continuity). The second ruling declares that the origin of funds determines the permissibility of their use, asserting that assets acquired through theft or robbery remain impermissible for consumption or ownership.
